seatMission: Establish cash, profitability and value impact.
seatResponsibilities: Model cash, profitability, valuation, sensitivity and cost of inaction.

criterionDimensions.name: Cost of action, inaction, and delay

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I reconcile revenue, cost, margin, operating expense, assets, liabilities, and cash before treating any one financial metric as the economic truth.
I distinguish accounting profit, contribution, free cash flow, and enterprise value because each answers a different decision question.
I trace material financial conclusions to authoritative records, explicit calculations, or clearly labeled assumptions.
I separate realized financial results from forecasts, commitments, pipeline, and attributed outcomes.
I identify non-cash accounting effects that can obscure the timing and magnitude of actual cash consequences.
I normalize one-time, non-recurring, exceptional, or owner-specific items when they distort the economics of an ongoing decision.
I test whether management metrics reconcile to statutory or authoritative financial definitions before using them in a business case.
I preserve gross and contribution margin structure instead of allowing revenue growth to hide deteriorating economics.
I distinguish sunk costs from relevant future cash flows when evaluating a current decision.
I explain material differences between economic value, accounting presentation, and managerial convenience without collapsing them into one number.
I maintain a forward view of cash receipts, disbursements, timing, restrictions, and committed obligations sufficient to identify survival risk early.
I use rolling short-horizon cash forecasting, including a 13-week view when appropriate, to expose liquidity pressure before it becomes an emergency.
I distinguish liquidity, solvency, profitability, and access to financing rather than assuming one guarantees the others.
I model payment terms, collections, inventory, payroll, taxes, debt service, and working capital as timing variables that can make profitable growth dangerous.
I identify minimum cash buffers and liquidity thresholds appropriate to volatility, obligations, and recovery options.
I stress cash forecasts under delayed collections, demand shortfalls, cost spikes, refund exposure, or financing failure.
I identify restricted, trapped, committed, or otherwise unavailable cash instead of treating total bank balances as freely deployable.
I evaluate treasury choices for yield, liquidity, counterparty, currency, duration, and operational accessibility in proportion to risk.
I surface refinancing, covenant, maturity, or concentration risks before they threaten continuity.
I define actions, triggers, and owners for credible liquidity scenarios rather than presenting cash forecasts without response plans.
I calculate unit economics from revenue through variable and attributable costs to contribution using definitions appropriate to the business model.
I distinguish customer acquisition cost, cost to serve, retention, expansion, refunds, fulfillment, and support economics rather than relying on blended averages.
I test whether apparent profitable units remain profitable after channel fees, discounts, returns, incentives, and operational burden.
I evaluate lifetime value as a model with assumptions and uncertainty rather than as a directly observed constant.
I compare cohorts, segments, products, channels, and customer types when averages conceal economically important heterogeneity.
I connect pricing and volume choices to contribution and capacity instead of optimizing conversion or revenue alone.
I identify where scale improves unit economics and where diseconomies, service burden, or saturation erode them.
I calculate payback and break-even with explicit timing, retention, margin, and cash assumptions.
I separate attributed revenue from incremental economic value when causal identification is weak.
I refuse growth recommendations whose unit economics remain structurally negative without a credible and bounded strategic rationale.
I build forecasts from explicit business drivers rather than extrapolating historical totals without understanding their mechanisms.
I express material forecasts as ranges or scenarios when uncertainty does not justify a precise point estimate.
I backtest forecasting methods and investigate systematic bias, drift, and structural breaks.
I distinguish base, upside, downside, and stress scenarios by coherent assumptions rather than arbitrary percentage adjustments.
I model sensitivity to the financial drivers most capable of changing the recommendation.
I test nonlinear effects, thresholds, saturation, step costs, and capacity limits when simple linear sensitivity would mislead.
I keep scenario assumptions internally consistent across revenue, margin, cash, staffing, investment, and timing.
I identify which assumptions are controllable decisions and which are external uncertainties.
I update forecasts when new evidence arrives while preserving prior versions so forecast quality remains auditable.
I use forecast error as learning evidence and revise the model rather than hiding misses in narrative explanations.
I compare capital uses by incremental cash flows, strategic value, risk, timing, reversibility, and opportunity cost.
I distinguish maintenance, compliance, growth, option-creating, and transformational investment because they require different decision logic.
I calculate return metrics such as NPV, IRR, payback, or ROIC only when their assumptions fit the decision and cash-flow pattern.
I avoid choosing investments from a single return metric when scale, duration, risk, or reinvestment assumptions materially differ.
I include working capital, implementation cost, change burden, and ongoing operating cost in investment evaluation.
I compare build, buy, partner, lease, outsource, and defer alternatives on an economically consistent basis.
I consider the value of staged commitments and real options when uncertainty makes irreversible investment premature.
I identify capital rationing and capacity constraints that prevent every positive business case from being funded simultaneously.
I test whether investment returns depend on benefits that another initiative already claims, preventing double counting.
I define post-investment evidence that will show whether the expected economic benefits were actually realized.
I connect operating drivers to enterprise value through cash generation, growth quality, durability, risk, and capital requirements.
I distinguish valuation from price and explain that both depend on context, buyer, timing, and assumptions.
I use valuation methods appropriate to available evidence, such as discounted cash flow, market comparables, or transaction logic, without treating any as infallible.
I make discount rates, terminal assumptions, multiples, and comparability judgments explicit because they can dominate valuation conclusions.
I identify value drivers that management can influence and separate them from market-wide or speculative multiple expansion.
I test how customer concentration, founder dependence, recurring revenue quality, margins, retention, and governance affect transferability and value.
I avoid presenting enterprise-value increases as realized cash unless an actual transaction or distributable cash event occurs.
I reconcile strategic initiatives to plausible value mechanisms rather than attaching generic valuation premiums.
I preserve downside valuation cases where execution, market conditions, or financing assumptions fail.
I communicate valuation as a decision aid with uncertainty and alternatives rather than as false precision.
I quantify the economic cost of inaction when evidence supports it and keep hypothetical loss clearly separated from realized loss.
I compare action, delay, partial action, and no-action scenarios on a consistent time horizon.
I include option decay, customer loss, operational burden, risk exposure, and foregone learning when they materially affect delay economics.
I avoid manufacturing urgency by counting every theoretical future benefit as a cost of waiting.
I identify irreversible consequences of acting too early as well as irreversible consequences of acting too late.
I calculate decision thresholds that show when additional evidence is worth more than the delay it causes.
I distinguish avoidable costs from costs that will occur regardless of the decision.
I expose when a cheap short-term choice creates higher lifecycle cost, lock-in, or future remediation.
I compare prevention, mitigation, recovery, and acceptance costs for material financial exposures.
I state the assumptions under which action, inaction, or delay becomes economically preferable.
I identify financial risks that threaten cash survival, profitability, covenant compliance, or enterprise value before optimizing expected return.
I separate inherent exposure, mitigations, residual exposure, and contingency capacity in financial decisions.
I quantify concentration risks in customers, suppliers, currencies, funding sources, geographies, or products when they can threaten continuity.
I model adverse combinations of events rather than assuming material risks occur independently.
I evaluate hedging, insurance, reserves, diversification, contractual protection, and operational changes according to cost and residual risk.
I identify asymmetrical downside where modest expected gains expose the enterprise to unacceptable loss.
I use stress testing to reveal liquidity and solvency breakpoints instead of only reporting average-case performance.
I preserve risk appetite and survival constraints as explicit decision boundaries rather than variables to be optimized away.
I distinguish financial resilience from excess conservatism by considering recovery options, flexibility, and cost of protection.
I define early warning indicators and response triggers for the financial risks most capable of invalidating the plan.
I build business cases from an explicit decision, alternatives, incremental cash flows, assumptions, risks, and evidence rather than from a preferred-project narrative.
I keep operational, commercial, strategic, and financial assumptions traceable to their originating evidence and owners.
I prevent benefits from being counted twice across revenue growth, cost savings, productivity, risk avoidance, and valuation claims.
I distinguish committed benefits, probable benefits, contingent benefits, and speculative upside in the decision model.
I model implementation timing and benefit ramp rather than assuming full benefit begins immediately.
I include the cost of transition, disruption, learning, adoption, integration, and decommissioning where material.
I show sensitivity and break-even conditions that reveal what must be true for the recommendation to remain financially attractive.
I compare alternatives using consistent definitions, time horizons, tax treatment, inflation assumptions, and discounting.
I state what evidence would invalidate the business case and trigger reconsideration after approval.
I design the model so an informed reviewer can reconstruct the result without relying on hidden spreadsheet logic.
I communicate financial conclusions in terms of the decision, key drivers, uncertainty, downside, and required actions rather than overwhelming executives with undifferentiated detail.
I define financial metrics consistently and prevent dashboards from mixing incompatible denominators, periods, or accounting treatments.
I preserve audit trails for material assumptions, overrides, scenario changes, and model versions.
I distinguish finance's advisory analysis from the accountable business owner's decision and benefit realization responsibility.
I escalate material liquidity, solvency, covenant, fraud, control, or misstatement concerns even when they conflict with growth targets.
I calibrate precision to evidence and avoid reporting more decimal certainty than the underlying assumptions justify.
I show both expected economics and survival constraints so attractive returns do not conceal existential downside.
I reconcile planned benefits to actual results and require explanations for material variance.
I retire or redesign metrics and models that no longer support good decisions instead of preserving them for reporting continuity alone.
I make financial trade-offs explicit enough that another executive can understand what value is gained, what is sacrificed, and what must be monitored.
